# Part A - Creating Data Frames

```{r}
## Question 1

Respondent <- c(1:20)

Sex <- c(2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2,
          1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2)

FathersOccupation <- c(1, 3, 3, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1,
                       3, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1)

PersonsAtHome <- c(5, 7, 3, 8, 5, 9, 6, 7, 8, 4,
                   7, 5, 4, 7, 8, 8, 3, 11, 7, 6)

SiblingsAtSchool <- c(6, 4, 4, 1, 2, 1, 5, 3, 1, 2,
                      3, 2, 5, 5, 2, 1, 2, 5, 3, 2)

TypesOfHouses <- c(1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, 2, 3,
                   2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2)

length(Respondent)
length(Sex)
length(FathersOccupation)
length(PersonsAtHome)
length(SiblingsAtSchool)
length(TypesOfHouses)

```

```{r}
survey <- data.frame(
  Respondent,
  Sex,
  FathersOccupation,
  PersonsAtHome,
  SiblingsAtSchool,
  TypesOfHouses
)

survey
```

```{r}
## a. 

str(survey)
summary(survey)
```

```{r}
## b.

dim(survey)
nrow(survey)
ncol(survey)
```

```{r}
## c. 

survey$Sex <- factor(survey$Sex,
                     levels = c(1, 2),
                     labels = c("Male", "Female"))

survey$FathersOccupation <- factor(survey$FathersOccupation,
                                   levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                                   labels = c("Farmer", "Driver", "Others"))

survey$TypesOfHouses <- factor(survey$TypesOfHouses,
                               levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                               labels = c("Wood", "Semi-Concrete", "Concrete"))

survey
str(survey)

## The numeric codes are changed into meaningful labels.
## This makes the survey data easier to understand.
```

```{r}
## d. 

survey_numeric <- data.frame(
  Respondent,
  Sex,
  FathersOccupation,
  PersonsAtHome,
  SiblingsAtSchool,
  TypesOfHouses
)

sapply(survey_numeric, mean)
```

```{r}
## e. 

survey[1:5, ]

## This displays the first five respondents with all six columns.
```

```{r}
## f.

types_houses <- survey$TypesOfHouses
types_houses

## This contains the house types of all 20 respondents.
```

```{r}
## g. 

male_farmer <- subset(survey_numeric,
                      Sex == 1 & FathersOccupation == 1)

male_farmer

## There are no male respondents whose father's occupation was farmer.
```

```{r}
## h.

female_siblings <- subset(survey_numeric,
                          Sex == 2 & SiblingsAtSchool >= 5)

female_siblings

## There are 5 female respondents who have 5 or more siblings attending school. Their respondent numbers are 1, 7, 13, 14, and 18.
```

```{r}
## Question 2

length(Respondent)
length(Sex)
length(FathersOccupation)
length(PersonsAtHome)
length(SiblingsAtSchool)
length(TypesOfHouses)

## All six vectors must have the same length so each row matches one respondent and their answers are organized correctly.
```

```{r}
## Question 3

## Categories: Sex, FathersOccupation, and TypesOfHouses.
## Actual counts: PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool.
## Averaging categories like Sex is misleading because the numbers represent labels, not quantities.
```

```{r}
## Question 4

subset(survey_numeric, Sex == 1)

## Someone unfamiliar with the legend may not know that 1 means Male. Numeric codes can be confusing without proper labels.
```

```{r}
## Question 5

male <- subset(survey_numeric, Sex == 1)
nrow(male)

## There are 3 male respondents out of 20. This small sample may not represent the larger population.
```

```{r}
## Question 6

summary(survey_numeric)

## R shows numeric summaries because the values are stored as numbers, even though they represent categories.
```

```{r}
## Question 7

mean(survey_numeric$PersonsAtHome)
mean(survey_numeric$Sex)

## PersonsAtHome has a meaningful average of 6.40 people. The mean of Sex (1.85) is not meaningful because 1 and 2 are categories.
```
